{{Short description|Siouan language of the Dhegihan group once spoken by the Kaw people}} {{about|the Siouan language of the United States|the Gur language spoken in Burkina Faso|Kaansa language}} {{Infobox language | name = Kansa | nativename = {{lang|ksk|Kaáⁿze Íe}} | states = [[United States]] | region = [[Kansas]], [[Oklahoma]] | ethnicity = [[Kaw people]] | extinct = 1983, with the death of Walter Kekahbah{{r|Ranney}} | revived = {{circa|12}} [[second language|L2]] speakers (2007) | ref = e18 | familycolor = American | fam1 = [[Siouan languages|Siouan]] | fam2 = [[Western Siouan languages|Western Siouan]] | fam3 = Mississippi Valley | fam4 = [[Dhegihan languages|Dhegiha]] | fam5 = Kansa–Osage | iso3 = ksk | linglist = qlc | lingname = Kansa-Osage | glotto = kans1243 | glottorefname = Kansa | map2 = Lang Status 01-EX.svg | mapcaption2 = {{center|Kansa is classified as Extinct by the [[UNESCO]] ''[[Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger]]''.}}{{cite report |title=Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger |publisher=UNESCO |edition=3rd |url=https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000187026 |date=2010 |page=11}} }} {{Infobox ethnonym|root=|people=[[Kaw people|Kaáⁿze]]|language=[[Kansa language|Kaáⁿze Íe]]|country=Mozhóⁿ Kaáⁿze}} '''Kansa''' ([[endonym|native name]]: ''Kaáⁿze Íe''),{{cite web |title=Kaáⁿze Íe – Kanza Language |url=https://www.kawnation.gov/language/ |website=Kaw Nation – People of the South Wind |publisher=Kaw Nation |access-date=17 October 2025}} sometimes known as '''Kaw''' or '''Kanza''', is a [[Siouan language]] of the [[Dhegihan languages|Dhegihan]] group once spoken by the [[Kaw people|Kaw]] people of [[Oklahoma]]. [[Charles Curtis|Vice President Charles Curtis]] spoke Kansa as a child. The last mother-tongue speaker, Walter Kekahbah, died in 1983.{{r|Ranney}} ==Classification== Kansa is a [[Dhegihan languages|Dhegiha Siouan language]], a broader category containing other languages such as [[Quapaw language|Quapaw]], [[Omaha–Ponca language|Omaha–Ponca]], and [[Osage language|Osage]]. This group of languages falls under Mississippi Valley Siouan, which is grouped under the largest category of the [[Siouan language family]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kawnation.com/WebKanza/LangPages/langkanza.html|title=WebKanza - KANZA|website=www.kawnation.com|access-date=2017-05-01|archive-date=2017-01-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170107140830/http://www.kawnation.com/WebKanza/LangPages/langkanza.html|url-status=dead}} ==History== The speakers of Kansa, known as the Kaw people, lived together with the Siouan-speakers in a united nation known as the Dhegiha Siouan group. This group was originally situated north of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River and then moved west down the Ohio River. Following their westward migration, the Dhegiha Siouan group branched into five indigenous ''tribes'' (Sioux subgroups) known mainly as Ponca, Osage, Omaha, Quapaw or Kaw people. Later on, many Kaw people migrated west of Missouri river and were called "People of the Southwind."{{Cite web|url=https://www.kshs.org/kansapedia/kaws-or-kanzas-kansas/17371|title=Kaws (or Kanzas, Kansas) - Kansapedia - Kansas Historical Society|website=www.kshs.org|language=en|access-date=2017-05-01}} The languages of the five tribes originating from the single Dhegiha group are quite similar, and have been regarded as dialects of each other. ==Geographic distribution== {{unref section|date=January 2026}} The Kansa Sioux language was mostly spoken in the U.S. state of Kansas.{{cn|date=August 2025}} ==Scholarship and resources== Pioneering anthropologist and linguist [[James Owen Dorsey]] collected 604 Kansa words in the 1880s and also made about 25,000 entries in a Kansa-English dictionary which has never been published.Unrau, William E. ''The Kansa Indians: A History of the Wind People, 1673-1873''. Norman: U of OK Press, 1971, p. 12 Dorsey also collected 24 narratives, historical accounts, and personal letters from nine Kansa speakers.''Kaanze Weyaje: Kanza Reader''. Kanza Language Project, Kaw City, OK: Kaw Nation, 2010, p. xiii In 1974, linguist [[Robert L. Rankin]] met Walter Kekahbah (d. 1983), Ralph Pepper (d. 1982), and Maud McCauley Rowe (d. 1978), the last surviving native speakers of Kansa. Rankin made extensive recordings of all three, especially Rowe, and his work over the next 31 years documented the language and helped the Kaw Nation to develop language learning materials.[http://www2.ljworld.com/news/2005/aug/01/researchers_try_preserve_indian_languages? Ranney, Dave. “Researchers try to preserve Indian languages.”], accessed 12 Apr 2011 == Language revitalization == Kansa has no native speakers. Members of the tribe now use English, while some still understand certain Kansa phrases and words. As part of a broader trend toward Native [[language revitalization]] efforts, the Kaw Nation offers online language learning for Kansa second language speakers (as of 2012). The 2nd Annual Dhegiha Gathering in 2012 brought Kansa, [[Quapaw language|Quapaw]], [[Osage language|Osage]], [[Omaha language|Omaha]] and [[Ponca language|Ponca]] speakers together to share best practices in language revitalization.{{Cite web |title=Dhegiha Gathering Agenda, 2012 |url=http://www.osagetribe.com/language/uploads/2ndAnnual-Agenda20120724.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130606080511/http://www.osagetribe.com/language/uploads/2ndAnnual-Agenda20120724.pdf |archive-date=2013-06-06 |access-date=2012-09-22}} ==Phonology== Kansa has 29 consonants and 8 vowels.{{Cite web|url=http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/sites/secure.lsit.ucsb.edu.ling.d7/files/sitefiles/research/papers/20/SBPL20_McBride.pdf|title=Orthography and Ideology: Examining the Development of Kaw Writing|last=McBride|first=Justin T.|access-date=2017-02-23}} {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |+Consonants ! colspan="2" | ![[Bilabial consonant|Bilabial]] ![[Dental consonant|Dental]] ![[Alveolar consonant|Alveolar]] ![[Postalveolar consonant|Post-

The number of a particular noun can be determined from the verb, an article or from context. For example, the word {{lang|ksk|sínga}} could be translated to English as "squirrel" or "squirrels" depending on context, in the sentence {{lang|ksk|Sínga miⁿ aⁿdómbabe}}, ({{Translation|We looked at a squirrel}}), it must be a single squirrel because of the article {{lang|ksk|miⁿ}}. ===Verbs=== Kansa is a [[Morphosyntactic alignment|SOV]] language and the verbs are [[Grammatical conjugation|inflected]] based on the person and number of their [[Grammatical subject|subjects]] and [[Direct object|objects]]. For example, in the sentence {{lang|ksk|ni kóⁿbla}} ({{Translation|I want water}}), the object {{wikt-lang|ksk|ni}}, ({{Translation|water}}), comes before the verb {{lang|ksk|kóⁿbla}} ({{Translation|I want}}). Kansa does not have [[verb tense]]s.{{dubious|date=June 2025}} ==Vocabulary== {{Expand section|date=September 2025}} Kansa has a great deal of vocabulary in common with the other languages of the Dhegiha Siouan group.
